name: Etretinate

lead: Etretinate was an oral vitamin A-derived drug for severe psoriasis, approved in the US in 1986 and withdrawn in the late 1990s.
It treated skin disease and was not a cosmetic; it has been replaced by acitretin.

paras: It converts to acitretin and binds retinoid receptors to normalise skin-cell maturation. It is stored in body fat and has a half-life of about 120 days.
Because it persists for years, birth-defect risk lasts long after treatment. Other effects include dry skin and lips and bone or joint pain. It is no longer sold in the US or Canada.

lead: Etretinate (brand names Tegison, Tigason) is a second-generation oral retinoid developed by Hoffmann-La Roche for severe psoriasis and related keratinisation disorders. The US FDA approved it in 1986, and Roche voluntarily withdrew it from the Canadian market in 1996 and the US market in 1998 because of its very long elimination half-life and teratogenic potential.[1][2] Wikipedia lists it as still marketed in Japan.[1]
Its successor is acitretin, the free acid and an active metabolite, which has a much shorter half-life.[1][2] Etretinate is a treatment for skin disease rather than a cosmetic agent.

paras: Etretinate was used for severe recalcitrant psoriasis, including pustular and erythrodermic types, and for ichthyosis, Darier disease and pityriasis rubra pilaris.[2][3] Reviews of retinoid therapy describe it alongside isotretinoin as one of the synthetic retinoids that made oral treatment of severe skin disease feasible.[4][5] It was also explored for chemoprevention of skin cancer and in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, with evidence limited to small studies.[2]

Effects resemble hypervitaminosis A: dry lips and skin, bone or joint pain, muscle cramps and dry eyes, with long-term use associated with hyperostosis.[1][2] Teratogenicity was a central concern. Etretinate is lipophilic, is stored in fat, and can be detectable in plasma for up to three years after therapy, so birth defects have been a risk long after treatment ends.[1] Former users are barred from donating blood in several countries.[1] A 1986 review of vitamin A congeners recorded the teratogenic pattern seen with the retinoid class.[6]

Etretinate is metabolised to acitretin and acts on retinoid receptors to normalise keratinocyte differentiation.[1][2] Its elimination half-life of roughly 120 days and low therapeutic index made dosing difficult.[1] Acitretin can be partly converted back into etretinate in the body, which is the reason given for long pregnancy-avoidance periods after acitretin.[1][2]

Roche developed etretinate and the FDA approved it as Tegison in 1986.[1][2] Withdrawal followed in Canada (1996) and the United States (1998), and acitretin was approved in the US in 1996 as a replacement.[1][2]

Published clinical literature on etretinate is mostly from the 1980s and 1990s and is summarised in pharmacology and therapeutic reviews of retinoids.[4][5] Those reviews address psoriasis, ichthyoses and other hyperkeratotic disorders. No studies of etretinate for cosmetic purposes were found.

timeline.event: Withdrawn in Canada; acitretin approved in the US.[1][2]
